title: Permutations and Combinations
seo_title: Permutations and Combinations Worksheet with Probability | 100 Questions with Answers
standard_text: Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems.
meta_desc: Free precalculus worksheet on permutations and combinations: the counting principle, nPr, nCr, arrangements with repeated letters and probability by counting. 100 questions.
key_big: Order matters: permutation. Order does not matter: combination.
key_sub: nPr = n!/(n − r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!).
body_html:
How it works

  • Counting principle: if one choice has m options and another has n, together there are m × n.
  • Permutation (order matters): nPr = n! / (n − r)!. Use it for rankings, roles, arrangements.
  • Combination (order does not matter): nCr = n! / (r!(n − r)!). Use it for groups, committees, hands.
  • Arranging letters with repeats: divide n! by the factorial of each repeat count.
  • Probability = (number of favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes), counted the same way.
Example

How many ways can a president and a treasurer be chosen from 10 people?

Order matters (different roles)

10 × 9

Answer: 90

Example

How many 3-person teams can be chosen from 10 people?

Order does not matter

10C3 = 720 ÷ 6

Answer: 120

Common mistakes

  • Adding the choices instead of multiplying.
  • Using a permutation for a group with no order. That counts each group several times.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated letters.
  • Allowing repeats when the problem says no repeats.

faq.q: What is the difference between a permutation and a combination?
faq.a: In a permutation the order matters (like first, second and third place). In a combination it does not (like choosing a committee).

faq.q: What is the formula for nCr?
faq.a: nCr = n! / (r!(n − r)!). It equals nPr divided by r!, because each group of r can be ordered in r! ways.

faq.q: How do you count arrangements of a word with repeated letters?
faq.a: Divide the factorial of the number of letters by the factorial of each letter's count. BANANA has 6!/(3! · 2!) = 60 arrangements.

faq.q: How do you use counting in probability?
faq.a: Count the favorable outcomes and the total outcomes the same way, then divide.

items.q: In a lottery, you choose 3 different numbers from 1 to 20, in any order. What is the probability that your numbers match the winning numbers?
